physics-electricity.essentialQuestion: For an ideal 12 V source across a 6 ohm resistor, what are the current and dissipated power, and what changes if resistance doubles?
physics-electricity.verifiedBoundary: Voltage is electric potential difference, current is the rate of charge flow, and resistance characterizes opposition to current in a component or material.

reasoningSteps: Frame the controlled model: A synthetic DC circuit contains an ideal 12 V source and one constant 6 ohm resistor with no other load or wire resistance. The learner must distinguish stated conditions from a physical measurement or an observed production device.

Derive the relevant quantity with its sign and unit: Use I=V/R to obtain amperes and P=VI (equivalently V squared/R) for dissipated watts. Explain why the chosen equation applies under the model assumptions.

Complete the numerical or logical work without a calculator black box: I=12/6=2 A; P=12 times 2=24 W, agreeing with I squared times R=4 times 6=24 W. Independently check dimensions or conservation when possible.

Stress-test the model by varying one input: Replace the resistor with 12 ohms while holding the ideal source at 12 V. Predict before checking the algebra, and compare against this expected result: I becomes 1 A and P becomes 12 W, rather than staying at the original 24 W.

Confront an attractive but incorrect inference: The claim that a resistor always receives 12 A because the source says 12 V confuses potential difference with charge per second. Show precisely which assumption, mathematical law, sign or unit disproves it.

State the evidence boundary before generalizing: This is an ideal steady-state ohmic model; resistor temperature coefficients, supply internal resistance and rating limits are not modeled. physics-v10-configuration-lab-capacitanc.analogy: Analogy — not literal: a physical model is like a carefully labeled map that leaves out some detail to make a relationship easier to study. The map is not the territory; equations, measurements, and cited evidence define the claim.

reasoningSteps: State the idealized boundaries: constant linear capacitance of 100 microfarads, negligible leakage, no series resistance and a fixed-voltage battery, not an isolated charged capacitor.
Translate 100 microfarads into 0.000100 farad; at 12 V, Q=CV=0.00120 C = 1.20 mC. Check that farads times volts really gives coulombs.
Use energy U=(1/2)CV^2, not QV without the factor one-half: 0.5*0.000100*12^2 = 0.00720 J; derive rather than memorize the energy scaling.
With C fixed and the source set to 6 V, charge becomes 0.000600 C while stored energy becomes 0.00180 J; charge halves but energy falls to one-quarter.
Challenge an isolated device: disconnect at 12 V with negligible leakage, then Q remains constant instead of V; any plate-spacing change requires recalculating the potential.
Explain why dielectric tolerance, probe loading and leakage could defeat the ideal predictions and separate the equation's proved scope from an empirical hardware claim.

labPlan: Make a wholly synthetic two-row table with fixed C=100 microfarads and battery settings of 12 V and 6 V; label Q in coulombs and U in joules.
Before revealing formulas, predict the ratios of Q and stored U between rows; justify why quadratic voltage dependence gives an energy ratio of 1/4.
Compute Q=0.00120 C and U=0.00720 J at 12 V using both U=CV^2/2 and U=QV/2, confirming identical results via independent expressions.
Repeat at 6 V for Q=0.000600 C and U=0.00180 J; disprove the shortcut that halving voltage must halve energy by comparing actual ratios.
Use a control scenario in which an ideal charged capacitor is disconnected with no leakage; show why a spontaneous 6 V claim at fixed C violates constant charge.

Check https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/8-3-energy-stored-in-a-capacitor for electrostatic field energy and the equivalence of U=QV/2 and CV^2/2; explicitly identify every number as illustrative, not measured.

physics-v10-reasoning-check-electric-cur.verifiedBoundary: Electric current is the rate at which electric charge passes through a surface.
physics-v10-reasoning-check-electric-cur.analogy: Analogy — not literal: a physical model is like a carefully labeled map that leaves out some detail to make a relationship easier to study. The map is not the territory; equations, measurements, and cited evidence define the claim.

reasoningSteps: Define the conductor cross-section, the reference current direction and a full 0.20-second observation window; current is flow rate, not stored charge.
Use I_average=delta Q/delta t for a synthetic 0.60 C transfer over 0.20 s to compute 3.0 A; verify 1 ampere equals 1 coulomb per second.
Split the interval into equal 0.10-second windows with 0.12 C and 0.48 C: the average in each subinterval is respectively 1.2 A and 4.8 A.
Compare the 3.0 A aggregate with the distinct stage currents; the full-window average alone does not define a constant waveform or instantaneous I(t).
Swap the two subintervals: total transferred charge and overall average remain unchanged, while the time history reverses; this is a constructive counterexample.
Distinguish conventional current from negative charge-carrier drift and note that instrument sampling intervals can conceal transients rather than prove uniform flow.

labPlan: Prepare a fictional transfer log with two rows: 0.12 C during 0-0.10 s, and 0.48 C during 0.10-0.20 s, with a consistent sign convention.
Predict whether a single 0.60 C/0.20 s figure uniquely determines instantaneous current, then write a hypothesis that a staged log could falsify.
Calculate separate averages 0.12/0.10=1.2 A and 0.48/0.10=4.8 A, then use total charges and times to recover the overall 3.0 A.
Swap row order without changing either charge or duration; verify the 3.0 A full-window average persists despite a different current-time history.
Run an unequal-duration control of 0.05 s and 0.15 s; show why the unweighted arithmetic mean of their average currents need not equal total Q/total t.

Compare the definitions I_average=delta Q/delta t and I=dQ/dt in https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-1-electrical-current; use invented teaching data, never represent these as oscilloscope measurements.

physics-v10-fault-isolation-lab-kirchhof.essentialQuestion: For a fictitious 12 V source and series resistors of 2 and 4 ohms, what can a 0.5 V loop discrepancy tell us, and what can it not establish?
physics-v10-fault-isolation-lab-kirchhof.verifiedBoundary: Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws express conservation of charge and energy in lumped electrical circuits.
physics-v10-fault-isolation-lab-kirchhof.analogy: Analogy — not literal: a physical model is like a carefully labeled map that leaves out some detail to make a relationship easier to study. The map is not the territory; equations, measurements, and cited evidence define the claim.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Kirchhoff’s current and voltage laws express conservation of charge and energy in lumped electrical circuits.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: State assumptions, draw or describe the model, keep units visible, and compare the result with the cited physical relationship. Construct a fictional failure around Kirchhoff’s Circuit Laws. Narrow it from broad layer/category to one testable cause without changing multiple variables at once. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Draw one ideal lumped DC loop with a 12 V source and 2-ohm and 4-ohm series resistors, labeling positive traversal and source polarity.
The series resistance is 6 ohms, so the predicted current is 12/6=2 A; by the circuit topology that same current traverses both resistors.
Calculate the modeled voltage drops 2*2=4 V and 2*4=8 V; Kirchhoff's signed loop equation gives +12-4-8=0 V.
Using hypothetical drops of 4.0 V and 7.5 V with a presumed 12 V supply, calculate +12-4.0-7.5=+0.5 V; classify it as model disagreement.
Show one plausible alternative: if the source terminal actually reads 11.5 V, then +11.5-4.0-7.5=0 V; the residual cannot localize a defect.
Name rival assumptions: lead drop, source regulation, probe loading, wiring polarity, temperature and resistor tolerance; propose independent checks.

Recreate the worked example from memory, then compare it with the lesson.

labPlan: Construct a purely synthetic 12 V, 2-ohm plus 4-ohm series circuit table, without physical wiring or any claim that test equipment was operated.
Predict I and both component voltage drops; calculate 2 A, 4 V and 8 V and verify that the signed sum of potential changes is zero.
Introduce a fictitious pair of readings 4.0 V and 7.5 V; compute the residual +0.5 V and label it an inconsistency requiring investigation.
Control the supply assumption: substitute a measured terminal voltage of 11.5 V in the worksheet and show that the same readings close the loop.
Build a diagnostic table separating source, resistor, lead and measurement errors; give a distinct independent observation capable of discriminating each.

Verify the sign convention in https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-3-kirchhoffs-rules; record that this laboratory's numbers are invented and do not demonstrate a real-world circuit fault.

physics-v10-transfer-challenge-ohm-law.essentialQuestion: With an ideal fixed 9 V supply, why does changing a constant resistor from 3 to 6 ohms halve both its current and dissipation, and why not for a diode?
physics-v10-transfer-challenge-ohm-law.verifiedBoundary: For an ohmic material or component under conditions where resistance is constant, voltage and current satisfy V=IR.
physics-v10-transfer-challenge-ohm-law.analogy: Analogy — not literal: a physical model is like a carefully labeled map that leaves out some detail to make a relationship easier to study. The map is not the territory; equations, measurements, and cited evidence define the claim.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: For an ohmic material or component under conditions where resistance is constant, voltage and current satisfy V=IR.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: State assumptions, draw or describe the model, keep units visible, and compare the result with the cited physical relationship. Apply the verified rule for Ohm Law to a new hypothetical context. Identify which parts transfer directly and which require new evidence. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Declare a constant-voltage 9 V ideal source and linear fixed-temperature resistor; exclude regulator droop, lead resistance and nonlinear components.
For R=3 ohms, I=V/R=9/3=3 A and P=VI=27 W; cross-check power by the independent expression V^2/R=81/3=27 W.
At R=6 ohms with 9 V still held fixed, I=1.5 A while P=81/6=13.5 W; both ratios are one-half of their 3-ohm values.
If instead 3 A is held fixed, the voltage would change from 9 V to 18 V as R doubles, and P=I^2R increases from 27 W to 54 W.
A diode or filament need not have constant resistance across bias or temperature; asserting the ohmic 1.5 A prediction without an I-V model is invalid.
Explain how a sequence of voltage-current pairs and device ratings would test linearity, and why the computed 27 W is not an endorsement of real-world safety.

labPlan: Use an invented two-row constant-9 V model with resistors of 3 and 6 ohms; avoid connecting hardware and do not assume either resistor has adequate rating.
Before calculation, predict the current and power change; identify the hidden mistake in applying a constant-current formula to a fixed-voltage circuit.
Calculate 9/3=3 A and 9/6=1.5 A, then independently evaluate 9^2/3=27 W and 9^2/6=13.5 W to verify both modeled powers.
Run a different control explicitly fixing current at 3 A: compute 27 W and 54 W and describe why the changed supply condition reverses the power trend.
Sketch a qualitative nonlinear I-V response; explain why a single 3-ohm nominal value cannot justify the same extrapolation for an LED or heated filament.

Check the documented ohmic/non-ohmic distinction in https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/9-4-ohms-law, and clearly distinguish illustrative calculations from actual device measurements.

physics-v10-measurement-lab-kirchhoff-ju.essentialQuestion: For a junction with 2.40 A entering and two outgoing branch currents, how do a 0.25 A residual and 0.05 A per-reading error limits constrain a diagnosis?
physics-v10-measurement-lab-kirchhoff-ju.verifiedBoundary: The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a circuit junction is zero, expressing conservation of charge.
physics-v10-measurement-lab-kirchhoff-ju.analogy: Analogy — not literal: a physical model is like a carefully labeled map that leaves out some detail to make a relationship easier to study. The map is not the territory; equations, measurements, and cited evidence define the claim.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: The algebraic sum of currents entering and leaving a circuit junction is zero, expressing conservation of charge.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: State assumptions, draw or describe the model, keep units visible, and compare the result with the cited physical relationship. Define what you would measure to evaluate a Kirchhoff Junction Rule hypothesis. Separate the measurement from the conclusion and state what result would change your mind. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

reasoningSteps: Fix a single reference direction at a fictional DC junction: 2.40 A enters while 0.80 A and 1.60 A leave; arrows, not magnitudes alone, determine signs.
Apply conservation of charge: 2.40-0.80-1.60=0.00 A, an exact synthetic closure that is not itself a verified meter reading.
Change one outgoing figure to 1.35 A and recompute 2.40-0.80-1.35=+0.25 A; frame this as evidence of inconsistent inputs, not missing charge.
Assume each of three measurements has an absolute bounded error no larger than 0.05 A; adding their worst-case contributions gives 0.15 A.
The 0.25 A residual exceeds that deterministic 0.15 A bound, disproving the joint assumption of an ideal node and all error bounds, but not specifying the cause.
Do not transform the bounded-error inequality into a 95% confidence statement; correlated meters, timing, omitted branch currents and calibration all matter.

labPlan: Create invented incoming/outgoing current rows 2.40 A, 0.80 A and 1.60 A and annotate each with its directed arrow before computing a residual.
Verify the initial signed difference 2.40-0.80-1.60=0 A and identify its dependence on simultaneous steady-state sampling in the model.
Replace one outgoing sample with 1.35 A to get +0.25 A; list calibration, missing branch, polarity and time-alignment alternatives to physical charge loss.
Assign an illustrative absolute uncertainty bound of 0.05 A per reading and sum three bounds to 0.15 A; state why 0.25 A cannot be explained by these assumed bounds alone.
Try a negative control with second outgoing branch at 1.50 A: +0.10 A residual falls inside 0.15 A, so the result cannot reject the model using this simple bound.

Independently review https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-3-kirchhoffs-rules for Kirchhoff's junction law; treat the error limits and branch data as invented exercises, not real metrology.

physics-v10-counterexample-lab-kirchhoff.essentialQuestion: Why does +12-4-8=0 correctly describe a synthetic DC source and two resistors, while +12+4+8=24 is a polarity mistake rather than energy generation?
physics-v10-counterexample-lab-kirchhoff.verifiedBoundary: Kirchhoff’s loop rule follows energy conservation: the algebraic sum of potential changes around a closed circuit loop is zero.

reasoningSteps: Choose a closed clockwise path from a 12 V ideal source through 2-ohm and 4-ohm resistors in series; mark source polarity and conventional current.
From I=12/(2+4)=2 A obtain resistor drops 4 V and 8 V; the specified traversal crosses the source from negative to positive.
The source contributes +12 V while two resistors crossed along current give -4 V and -8 V: the algebraic closed-loop total is exactly zero.
The deliberately incorrect +12+4+8=24 V makes all terms voltage rises although the resistor polarities demand drops; it is a sign bookkeeping error.
Reversing traversal flips every sign, producing -12+4+8=0 V; reversing only the battery term would not represent the same physical path.
State the model boundary: this lumped DC electrostatic calculation does not license disregarding induction from a time-varying magnetic flux.

labPlan: Sketch a fictional DC 12 V source in series with 2 and 4 ohms; draw arrows and label polarities, not just unlabeled positive magnitudes.
Calculate the resulting current 2 A and separate drops 4 V and 8 V; write the clockwise loop equation +12-4-8=0 before seeing alternatives.
Evaluate the deliberately bad loop sum +12+4+8=24 V; identify the resistor polarity signs that were incorrectly assigned as positive.
Reverse the traversal consistently to produce -12+4+8=0 V, and explain why multiplying an entire valid loop equation by -1 preserves its solutions.
Replace the 4-ohm resistor with 3 ohms at constant 12 V; compute I=12/5=2.4 A and drops 4.8 V and 7.2 V, still closing the loop.

Check signed loop rules at https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/10-3-kirchhoffs-rules; explicitly describe the example as steady-state, lumped and synthetic, not as a measurement of an energized circuit.
